title: How Supersmart Ate the Elephant
summary: In a dense forest, an exceptionally shrewd jackal named Mahachatura, or Supersmart, was roaming in search of food when he discovered the ...
full_text:
In a dense forest, an exceptionally shrewd jackal named Mahachatura, or Supersmart, was roaming in search of food when he discovered the colossal carcass of an enormous wild elephant that had died of old age in a clearing.

The jackal was famished, but the elephant's hide was as thick and tough as cured iron, and his weak teeth could not pierce the leather. Sitting beside the mountain of meat, Supersmart pondered how to cut through the hide.

Presently, the great lion Pingalaka strode into the clearing. Supersmart immediately prostrated himself in the dust: 'O supreme Monarch of the Forest! I have slain this colossal elephant with great toil expressly for your royal table! Deign to accept this humble offering from your servant!'

The noble lion turned his head with aristocratic pride: 'I am the King of Beasts! I never eat prey slain by another! I bestow the carcass upon you, honest jackal!' With that, the lion departed.

Next, a greedy, treacherous tiger padded into the clearing. Supersmart put on a face of extreme terror: 'Uncle, flee for your life! The great King of Beasts slew this elephant and went to the river to bathe. Before he left, he commanded me: "Guard this carcass! If any tiger dares to touch a mouthful, tell me, and I will tear his stripes from his flesh!"'

Terrified of the lion's wrath, the cowardly tiger leaped into the bushes and vanished like the wind.

Next, a powerful leopard with razor-sharp claws entered the clearing. Supersmart thought: 'Here are the claws that can pierce the tough hide!'

Supersmart bowed: 'Welcome, nephew! You look famished. This elephant was slain by the lion, who has gone to drink. While he is absent, you may quickly tear open the hide and feast! The instant I see the lion returning, I will whistle, and you can escape!'

Delighted, the hungry leopard sprang upon the elephant and ripped the tough hide wide open.

Just as the tender meat was exposed, Supersmart shrieked: 'Run, nephew, run! The King of Beasts is coming!' Panicked, the leopard scrambled into the treetops and fled, leaving the opened meat behind.

Finally, another jackal arrived, hoping to share the spoils. Supersmart said to himself: 'Toward the lion, flattery; toward the tiger, fear; toward the leopard, deceit; but toward an equal, one must use force!'

Supersmart bristled his fur, bared his fangs, and attacked the rival jackal with such savage fury that the intruder fled howling into the ravine.

Alone in the clearing, the clever jackal feasted upon the delicious, tender meat for an entire month in luxury and peace.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Win over the noble with humble speech and courtly grace;
Defeat the cruel coward by the fear of higher place;
Beguile the foolish glutton with a cunning, poisoned bait;
And crush an equal adversary with decisive weight."
moral: He who lacks physical strength can use different tactics for different adversaries to secure the entire prize.

title: The Dog Who Went Abroad
summary: In a quiet village lived an honest street dog named Chitranga. A severe famine struck the province; food scraps vanished, and the village...
full_text:
In a quiet village lived an honest street dog named Chitranga. A severe famine struck the province; food scraps vanished, and the village dogs grew gaunt as skeletons.

Chitranga thought: 'If I remain here, I will starve to death. I will travel to a distant, foreign city where famine has not struck.'

Journeying across the mountains, he arrived at a prosperous foreign capital. In this rich metropolis, wealthy households threw out lavish platters of roasted meats, buttery pastries, and rice daily. Chitranga slipped into the courtyards every afternoon, feasting until his belly was round and his coat grew glossy and sleek.

Yet his life in this foreign paradise was a torment. The local dogs of the city were fiercely territorial, vicious, and hostile to strangers. Whenever Chitranga walked through the lanes, packs of local dogs ambushed him from every alley, barking savagely, biting his legs, tearing his ears, and slashing his flanks with their fangs. He was constantly running for his life, covered in bleeding wounds.

Licking his bleeding sores under a bridge, Chitranga reflected: 'What good is rich meat and buttery rice when every mouthful must be bought with terror, wounds, and hatred?'

Abandoning the foreign metropolis, Chitranga returned across the mountains to his native village.

His old companions gathered around him, marvelling at his sleek coat: 'Welcome home, brother! Tell us of foreign lands! How are the manners of foreign people, and what is the food like?'

Chitranga replied with profound wisdom:
"In foreign realms the food is rich, the buttered meats abound;
Within the courtyards of the rich delightful feasts are found;
Yet one supreme, tormenting curse within that land resides:
Your own kind tears you limb from limb wherever hatred hides!
Give me my humble homeland crust, where peaceful brethren dwell,
Far from the foreign luxury that turns a feast to hell."
moral: Foreign luxury accompanied by hostility and strife is far worse than humble peace in one's own homeland.

title: Ill-Considered Action (Frame)
summary: Pandit Vishnu Sharma gathered the three royal princes—Bahushakti, Ugrashakti, and Anantashakti—in the marble pavilion beneath the bloomin...
full_text:
Pandit Vishnu Sharma gathered the three royal princes—Bahushakti, Ugrashakti, and Anantashakti—in the marble pavilion beneath the blooming champaka trees. The young men, once restless and dull-witted, now listened with rapt attention as the revered master opened the fifth and final scroll of wisdom: Aparikshitakarakam, the treatise on Ill-Considered Action.

'Hearken well, noble sons of King Amarashakti,' the sage began in a voice like resonant temple chimes. 'You have mastered the art of discerning false friends in Mitra-bheda; you have witnessed the sacred power of loyal companions in Mitra-labha; you have studied the subtle statecraft of peace and war in Kakolukiyam; and you have learned how greed steals away hard-won treasures in Labdhapranasham.

'Now comes the most vital discipline of all: the mastery of the rash and impetuous mind. He who acts without thorough investigation, who allows rumors, anger, or sudden panic to strike before truth is weighed, strikes a dagger into his own chest. Neither exalted birth, nor vast wealth, nor formidable strength can rescue the monarch whose ministers act upon hasty conclusions.

'Consider the merchant who acted upon a dream, the barber who struck down holy mendicants because he misunderstood another's fortune, and above all, the grieving mother who slew the loyal mongoose before examining the cradle. Every catastrophe in the affairs of men stems from this single root: action without deliberation.'

With these words, Vishnu Sharma commenced the final cycle of tales, sealing the princes' education in the highest art of governance. As the opening verse proclaims:
"He who undertakes an action without testing well the ground,
Who leaps to sudden judgment where no evidence is found,
Shall mourn his hasty folly through the bitter years ahead,
Like the mother weeping hopelessly beside her infant's bed."
moral: He who acts in haste without investigation will mourn his folly through bitter years.

title: The Loyal Mongoose
summary: In a quiet village lived an impoverished, pious Brahmin named Devasarman and his devoted wife. For many years they prayed for a child, an...
full_text:
In a quiet village lived an impoverished, pious Brahmin named Devasarman and his devoted wife. For many years they prayed for a child, and at last the wife gave birth to a beautiful baby boy, who was the delight of their hearts.

Around that same time, a motherless baby mongoose was found shivering in the grass near their door. Moved by compassion, the Brahmin's wife adopted the little creature, nursing him alongside her baby son with equal tenderness. The child and the mongoose grew up together like brothers, playing upon the clean mats of the courtyard.

Yet a mother's natural anxiety remained in the woman's heart. She often thought: 'He is a wild animal by birth; his nature may suddenly assert itself and harm my tender babe.'

One afternoon, the Brahmin went to the village temple to perform a religious ceremony. The wife had to fetch fresh water from the river. Placing her sleeping infant securely in his wooden cradle, she turned to the mongoose and said: 'Watch over your little brother carefully, my child, while I am at the river.'

The faithful mongoose sat beside the cradle, watching with vigilant, amber eyes.

Presently, a monstrous, venomous black cobra slithered silently through a crack in the wall, gliding toward the baby's cradle with raised hood, ready to strike!

Seeing the deadly threat to his beloved foster brother, the brave mongoose sprang like lightning! With ferocious courage, he attacked the venomous serpent. A furious, desperate battle raged upon the floor: the snake hissed and struck with its fangs, but the agile mongoose dodged every blow, clamped his razor teeth behind the cobra's hood, and tore the reptile to shreds, saving the infant's life!

His mouth, paws, and chest covered with the dark blood of the slain serpent, the triumphant mongoose trotted to the threshold to greet his mother, eager to show his loyalty.

As the mother arrived carrying her heavy water-pot, she saw the mongoose sitting at the door, his jaws dripping with fresh blood!

In an instant of blind, unthinking horror, without checking the cradle, without examining the room, and without pausing to investigate, the terrified mother shrieked: 'Murderer! You have killed and devoured my only child!'

With all her might, she hurled the heavy, stone-hard earthenware water-pot squarely upon the little animal's head!

The heavy jar shattered; the water poured across the threshold, and the faithful mongoose lay dead upon the stones, his skull crushed by the hand of the mother he had served.

Weeping hysterically, the woman rushed into the bedchamber. To her astonishment, she beheld her baby boy sleeping peacefully in his cradle, smiling in his dreams, while beside the cradle lay the mangled carcass of the venomous black cobra, torn to pieces!

The horrific truth pierced the mother's soul like a flaming dagger. She had murdered the faithful, heroic protector of her son! Falling upon the dead mongoose, she tore her hair and wept bitter, inconsolable tears of remorse, but no tears could restore the breath to the loyal beast.

When the Brahmin returned, he found his wife weeping in agony beside the two carcasses, mourning her hasty folly for the rest of her days.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who acts in sudden anger ere the evidence is weighed,
Leaping blindly to conclusions by a hasty terror made,
Shall mourn the loyal guardian he struck down upon the floor,
And carry in his bleeding heart remorse for evermore."
moral: Never act upon sudden anger or hasty assumptions; look before you strike down a faithful protector.

title: The Four Treasure-Seekers
summary: In the ancient city of Avanti lived four young Brahmins who had lost their ancestral inheritances through misfortune. Refusing to endure ...
full_text:
In the ancient city of Avanti lived four young Brahmins who had lost their ancestral inheritances through misfortune. Refusing to endure the humiliation of poverty among their kin, they resolved to travel together to distant lands in search of fortune.

Journeying to the sacred peaks of the Vindhya mountains, they visited a renowned master of occult sciences, the sage Bhairavananda. Prostrating before him, they pleaded: 'Revered master! We have renounced our home; grant us the means to win wealth, or we will end our lives at your feet!'

Moved by their determination, the sage crafted four magical quills woven of mystic grass, handing one to each youth: 'Walk northward into the uninhabited mountains. Wherever a quill falls from your hand, dig into the earth at that exact spot, take whatever treasure you find, and return home in peace.'

The four companions set out. After walking several leagues, the quill of the first youth slipped from his fingers and tumbled upon the turf.

They dug into the soil and unearthed an inexhaustible vein of pure copper. The first youth rejoiced: 'Brothers, here is vast wealth! Let us load our sacks with copper and return home!'

The other three laughed: 'Copper is base and heavy! Only fools carry copper when gold lies ahead!' The first youth took his load of copper and turned homeward, content and rich.

The remaining three pressed onward. Soon, the quill fell from the hand of the second youth. They dug and uncovered a rich mine of solid silver!

The second youth cried: 'Silver is precious! Take all you can carry and let us return!'

The remaining two sneered: 'Silver is nothing compared to gold! We will press forward!' The second youth loaded his sacks with silver and returned home.

The two remaining companions pushed deeper into the wilderness. Soon, the quill fell from the hand of the third youth. Digging into the earth, they uncovered a dazzling hoard of pure, heavy gold!

The third youth was overjoyed: 'Gold is the king of metals! We need look no further; let us load our packs with gold dinars and return in splendor!'

The fourth youth, consumed by insatiable avarice, scoffed: 'Beyond copper lay silver; beyond silver lay gold; surely beyond gold lies the realm of celestial gems and diamonds! I will not turn back!'

The third youth warned him: 'Friend, gold is sufficient to banish poverty for seven generations! Do not tempt fate!' But the greedy companion walked forward alone into the scorched, desolate crags.

Under a blazing, brassy sun, parched with thirst, the fourth youth stumbled into a desolate plateau. There he saw a solitary man standing motionless upon a rock, his body bathed in blood, while upon his head whirled an enormous, razor-sharp wheel of burning iron, slicing perpetually into his skull!

The greedy youth approached and asked: 'Brother, why do you stand here with that burning wheel whirling upon your head? Where can I find water?'

The instant the words left his lips, the whirling wheel of burning iron sprang from the stranger's head and settled upon the head of the fourth youth, slicing into his skull with agonizing fire!

The youth shrieked in agony: 'Horror! What is this wheel? Why does it torment me?'

The bleeding stranger smiled in relief: 'I, too, possessed a magic quill and was blinded by insatiable greed! I rejected gold to seek diamonds, and arrived here to receive this wheel of torment! None can relieve you of this burning burden until another mortal, equally blinded by insatiable avarice, walks to this spot and questions you!' With that, the relieved stranger vanished.

Thus the greedy youth was left to whirl the wheel of torment through centuries of regret.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who knows when to halt his quest and take his golden prize,
Walks back to honor and to peace beneath the tranquil skies;
While he whose blind, insatiate greed still reaches for the sun,
Receives the burning wheel of pain where destiny is done."
moral: Blind and insatiable greed that rejects sufficient wealth leads straight to the wheel of perpetual torment.

title: The Lion-Makers
summary: In a flourishing university city in northern India lived four young Brahmins who had been companions since childhood. Three of them were ...
full_text:
In a flourishing university city in northern India lived four young Brahmins who had been companions since childhood. Three of them were scholars of prodigious intellect, having mastered the sacred scriptures, grammar, logic, and arcane esoteric sciences, but they were completely devoid of practical common sense. The fourth companion, named Subuddhi, or Good-Sense, had never studied ancient books, but possessed exceptional common sense and practical wisdom.

One day, the four youths resolved to travel to the courts of foreign kings to display their learning and win riches.

As they set out along the highway, the eldest scholar objected: 'Subuddhi has read no books; he has no scholarship! Why should we share the royal gifts with an uneducated companion? Let him return home!'

The second scholar agreed, but the third, who was generous, said: 'No, we have played together as brothers since our youth. Let him come; he shall receive his share of our earnings.'

As they walked through a dense forest, they came upon a clearing strewn with the dry, bleached bones of a dead beast.

The first scholar exclaimed: 'Here is an opportunity to demonstrate the miraculous power of our scientific learning! A creature lies dead before us; let us bring it back to life!'

The first scholar stepped forward: 'By the power of my knowledge of anatomy, I can assemble these scattered bones into their proper skeletal structure!' Chanting mantras, he assembled the skeleton: it was the complete skeleton of a colossal, ferocious lion!

The second scholar stepped forward: 'By my mastery of esoteric biology, I can clothe these bones with sinews, flesh, skin, and warm blood!' Chanting his spells, the bones were covered with muscular flesh, a bristling golden mane, and razor-sharp claws. The colossal beast lay upon the grass, complete in every feature, awaiting only the breath of life.

The third scholar stepped forward, raising his hands: 'Now, by the supreme science of vital animation, I will breathe the living soul into this frame!'

Seeing him prepare to animate the beast, the fourth companion, Subuddhi, seized his arm in alarm: 'Hold your hand, brother! Can you not see that this is a ferocious lion? If you bring this predator to life, he will instantly spring upon us and devour us all!'

The third scholar sneered with arrogant pride: 'Ignorant fool! Do you dare to forbid me from demonstrating the triumph of my scientific scholarship? I will not permit my learning to be wasted!'

Subuddhi replied calmly: 'If you are determined to create a monster, wait but a single minute until I have climbed into the high branches of yonder tree!'

Subuddhi scrambled up the trunk of a tall banyan tree, perching safely upon a stout bough.

The third scholar chanted his final, triumphant incantation. The breath of life entered the colossal beast: its golden eyes blazed; its nostrils flared, and with a thunderous roar that shook the forest, the famished lion sprang to its feet!

Seeing three fat, defenseless scholars standing before him, the ferocious beast leaped upon them with flashing claws, tearing all three learned men to pieces and devouring their flesh upon the spot.

Once the beast had eaten his fill and ambled away into the forest, Subuddhi climbed down from the tree in safety, returning home to his village, having learned that book-learning without common sense is fatal.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Better is common sense by far than books and scholarly pride;
For learning without practical wit is ruin at your side;
Behold the three great scholars dead upon the forest floor,
Slain by the very lion's fangs their learning brought to roar."
moral: Mere book-learning and scholarship without practical common sense leads to swift and certain destruction.

title: Hundred-Wit Thousand-Wit and Single-Wit
summary: In an expansive, crystal-clear mountain pool lived two large, magnificent fish named Shatabuddhi, or Hundred-Wit, and Sahasrabuddhi, or T...
full_text:
In an expansive, crystal-clear mountain pool lived two large, magnificent fish named Shatabuddhi, or Hundred-Wit, and Sahasrabuddhi, or Thousand-Wit. They were proud of their intellectual brilliance, boasting endlessly of their ability to outsmart any danger. In that same pool lived a humble, modest green frog named Ekabuddhi, or Single-Wit. The three were companions.

One evening, as they conversed near the bank, several fishermen passed along the shore carrying nets and baskets. Pointing to the water, the fishermen said: 'This pool is deep and full of fish. Tomorrow morning, let us bring our drag-nets and empty this water completely!'

When the fishermen departed, the humble frog Single-Wit trembled with alarm: 'Brothers! You heard the fishermen's threat. What shall we do? Shall we flee or stay?'

Thousand-Wit laughed with arrogant scorn: 'Do not be terrified by mere words, little frog! The world is full of threats that never materialize! Even if the fishermen come, I possess a thousand ingenious maneuvers of evasion—diving into subterranean mud, leaping through the meshes, and spinning behind boulders! I will protect you with my thousand wits!'

Hundred-Wit chimed in: 'And I possess a hundred proven strategies of escape! It is cowardly to abandon our ancestral pool before the net is cast! Stay and watch our genius!'

Single-Wit the frog replied with humble simplicity: 'Brothers, I possess neither a thousand wits nor a hundred wits; I possess only a single, simple wit, and my single wit tells me to flee danger before it strikes!'

That very evening, while the two clever fish mocked his cowardice, the frog took his wife and hopped through the grass to an adjoining stream, swimming safely away into the deep river.

At dawn, the fishermen arrived with their heavy drag-nets. Wading into the pool, they swept the water from end to end.

Thousand-Wit attempted his thousand maneuvers, and Hundred-Wit tried his hundred strategies, but the fine hemp mesh was relentless. Both brilliant fish were trapped, hauled onto the dry sands, and beaten to death with cudgels.

At noon, as the fishermen marched home along the riverbank, the frog Single-Wit peeked from beneath a lily pad. He saw the fishermen carrying Hundred-Wit upon their shoulders as a grand prize, while Thousand-Wit was tied to a string, dangling lifeless in the dust.

Turning to his wife, Single-Wit whispered:
"Behold the proud Thousand-Wit dangling in the dust,
And Hundred-Wit upon the pole, their cleverness nonplussed;
While Single-Wit, who fled the net with simple, humble speed,
Swims safely in the river pool among the water-weed."
moral: A single practical plan executed with swift decisiveness is far better than a thousand clever theories.

title: The Musical Donkey
summary: In a manufacturing town lived an impoverished washerman who owned an old, overworked donkey named Uddhata. During the day, the donkey car...
full_text:
In a manufacturing town lived an impoverished washerman who owned an old, overworked donkey named Uddhata. During the day, the donkey carried heavy loads of wet linen; but at night, the washerman set him loose to graze upon the roadside grass.

The donkey made friends with a cunning, night-roaming jackal. Every midnight, the two companions broke through the hedge of a wealthy farmer's irrigated garden, feasting on sweet, crisp cucumbers, watermelons, and ripe gourds until their bellies were round.

One moonlit night, having gorged himself on sweet cucumbers, the donkey felt an overwhelming surge of artistic ecstasy. Looking at the glorious full moon shining in the cloudless sky, the donkey said to the jackal: 'Nephew! Look at the celestial splendor of this night! The cool breeze is fragrant, the sky is sapphire, and my heart is overflowing with musical inspiration! I must sing a classical raga to celebrate this beauty!'

The jackal was horrified: 'Uncle, have you lost your senses? We are thieves inside another man's private garden! Your voice is not a sweet veena; it is a harsh, grating bray like a cracked conch! If you bray, the farmer and his watchmen will wake, rush out with heavy clubs, and beat us to death! Eat your cucumbers in silence!'

The donkey took fire with insulted vanity: 'Ignorant beast! You live in the wild woods and understand nothing of the fine arts! You dare to criticize my melodious voice? When I sing in the Gandharva style, the gods themselves listen with delight!'

The jackal replied: 'Very well, uncle. If you must sing, wait until I have slipped through the hedge and stationed myself outside on the road to watch for danger.'

The jackal slipped through the fence.

The donkey threw back his long ears, lifted his muzzle toward the moon, and unleashed his 'classical song' with all the power of his lungs: 'HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW!'

The deafening, discordant braying shattered the quiet night.

Awakened by the noise, the furious farmer and his watchmen leaped from their cots, armed with heavy wooden pestles and cudgels. Rushing into the garden, they found the donkey standing among the trampled cucumber vines, braying in artistic bliss.

The watchmen fell upon the foolish animal, beating him across his ribs and spine until he collapsed to the earth. To ensure he did not escape, they tied a heavy, jagged wooden mortar around his neck with a stout cord and left him groaning in the mud.

Crawling painfully through the broken hedge with the heavy mortar dragging between his legs, the donkey met the jackal waiting on the road.

The jackal chuckled:
"I warned you of the music, uncle, and the singer's pride;
Yet you would sing your moonlight song and wouldn't be denied;
Now wear the mortar as your prize, adorned with bruises sore,
And sing your midnight melodies upon the field no more!"
moral: Singing out of time and place brings only a beating; know when to be silent.

title: Slow the Weaver
summary: In a quiet village lived an honest, simple-minded weaver named Mantharaka, known to all as Slow because of his patient and compliant natu...
full_text:
In a quiet village lived an honest, simple-minded weaver named Mantharaka, known to all as Slow because of his patient and compliant nature. One day, while weaving a heavy carpet, the wooden frame of his ancestral loom cracked and splintered beyond repair.

Shouldering his axe, Slow walked into the forest to find a sturdy tree of seasoned timber to hew a new loom-beam. Wandering to the seashore, he found a majestic, ancient shisham tree, tall, straight, and branchless for thirty cubits.

As the weaver raised his iron axe to strike the trunk, a luminous tree spirit emerged from the bark and pleaded: 'Hold your blow, gentle artisan! This ancient tree is my sacred dwelling. If you spare my home, I will grant you any boon your heart desires!'

Slow lowered his axe, bowed politely, and said: 'Revered spirit, I must consult my dear friend and my beloved wife before I choose my wish. Remain here, and I will return shortly.'

Slow hurried to the village and visited his friend, the town barber. Explaining the spirit's offer, Slow asked: 'What should I ask for, brother?'

The barber's eyes gleamed with ambition: 'Ask to be made King of this realm! You can rule from a golden palace, and make me your grand vizier!'

Slow replied: 'Kingship is a burden of endless wars, conspiracies, and sleepless nights. Let me consult my wife; women have great wisdom in domestic affairs.'

The barber warned: 'Never consult a woman on great matters! Women think only of petty vanities!'

Yet Slow returned home and asked his wife: 'Dearest, the tree spirit has granted me a wish. The barber advises me to ask for a kingdom. What is your counsel?'

The wife scoffed: 'A kingdom? Kings are assassinated by their brothers or overthrown by rebellions! Ask for something practical for your trade! You are a weaver with only two hands and one head; ask for another head and two more hands! With four hands and two heads, you can operate two looms simultaneously, weave twice as many carpets, earn double profits, and become the richest merchant in the province without the perils of a crown!'

Pleased by her advice, Slow ran back to the forest and called out: 'O Tree Spirit! Grant me two heads and four hands, so that I may weave with double speed!'

'Your wish is granted!' spoke the spirit.

Instantly, a second head sprouted from Slow's neck, and two additional muscular arms grew from his shoulders!

Rejoicing, Slow marched proudly back into the village to display his marvelous new body to his neighbors.

As he entered the village square, the terrified villagers mistook the four-armed, two-headed apparition for a demonic Rakshasa invading their homes. Crying: 'A monster! A demon has entered the town!' they rushed upon him with iron bars, heavy stones, and clubs, beating poor Slow to death on the spot.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who takes counsel of a fool to shape his fortune's choice,
Ignoring reason, prudence, and the wise preceptor's voice,
Shall find the granted wish transform to ruin in a breath,
And bring the double-headed fool to an untimely death."
moral: Do not consult foolish or greedy advisers when a great opportunity is placed in your hands.

title: The Brahman's Dream
summary: In the city of Devakotta lived a notoriously lazy, penurious Brahmin named Svabhavakripana, or Miser by Nature. Living solely upon the ch...
full_text:
In the city of Devakotta lived a notoriously lazy, penurious Brahmin named Svabhavakripana, or Miser by Nature. Living solely upon the charity of pilgrims, he begged daily from door to door, saving every scrap of food. Having received a large earthenware jar filled to the brim with barley flour, he carried it home, tied a stout cord around its neck, and hung it from an iron peg driven into the wall directly above his sleeping cot.

Lying upon his bed with his eyes fixed upon the hanging jar, the Brahmin began to weave an extravagant daydream of future wealth:

'If a severe famine strikes this province,' mused the dreamer, 'I can sell this jar of barley flour for one hundred silver coins! With that silver, I will purchase a pair of healthy young she-goats. Every six months they will bear twin kids; within five years, I will possess a herd of three hundred goats!

'I will trade the goats for twenty cows and a bull; the cows will yield calves and milk, and I will become a wealthy dairyman! I will sell the cattle and purchase fifty mares, breeding fine warhorses to sell to the King's cavalry!

'With the gold from the horses, I will build a magnificent four-story palace of carved marble, with fountains and gardens. Observing my vast wealth, an honorable and wealthy Brahmin will approach me and offer his beautiful, accomplished daughter in marriage with an enormous dowry of rubies and silks!

'In due time, my lovely wife will give birth to a handsome son, whom I will name Somasarman. When the child is old enough to crawl, I will sit on the veranda reading sacred books. The boy will crawl toward the horse's stall; I will shout to my wife: "Take the child away!"

'Engrossed in household chores, she will fail to hear my command. In righteous anger at her disobedience, I will spring from my couch and kick her with all my might!'

Lost in the vivid fury of his daydream, the foolish Brahmin lashed out with his foot, kicking violently into the air!

His heavy heel struck the earthenware jar hanging from the peg above his cot. The jar shattered to pieces with a loud crash, and the entire hundred pounds of barley flour poured down upon the dreamer, choking his throat, blinding his eyes, and burying him in a heap of white dust.

Sitting in the ruins of his shattered pot, coughing up flour, the foolish Brahmin wept for his lost empire.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who builds palaces of air upon an idle bed,
Neglecting present duty for the dreams within his head,
Shall find his kicking folly break the jar that gave him bread,
And sit within the scattered dust with all his fortunes dead."
moral: Building castles in the air while neglecting reality brings sudden, self-inflicted loss.

title: The Unforgiving Monkey
summary: In the royal palace of King Chandra ruled a magnificent court where a large troop of wild monkeys was pampered as royal pets. The princes...
full_text:
In the royal palace of King Chandra ruled a magnificent court where a large troop of wild monkeys was pampered as royal pets. The princes fed them almonds, sugar-cane, and candied fruits, allowing them to roam freely through the gardens. The chief of the monkeys was an ancient, experienced patriarch named Chandra, deeply versed in philosophy and observation.

In the royal stables lived an arrogant, quarrelsome ram whose duty was to turn the waterwheel. The ram was voracious and frequently slipped into the royal kitchens to steal hot cakes and cooked rice. The furious cooks drove him away with firebrands, sticks, and boiling water.

Observing the ongoing feud, the old monkey patriarch pondered with grave concern: 'This conflict between the ram and the cooks will bring catastrophe! When the ram enters the kitchen, the cooks throw burning firebrands at him. If a burning stick catches the ram's thick wool, the blazing animal will run in panic into the adjoining stables, where dry grass and straw are stacked! The stables will catch fire; the King's prize horses will be burned, and according to the ancient treatises on veterinary medicine, there is only one sovereign remedy for burns upon horses: the fat of freshly slaughtered monkeys!'

Assembling his troop, the old patriarch warned: 'Brothers, leave this palace immediately! The ram and the cooks will burn the stables, and the physicians will slaughter us for our fat! Let us return to the safety of the mountain forests!'

The young, foolish monkeys laughed with scorn: 'Leave the palace? Abandon the sweet almonds, the sugar-cane, and the silk cushions of the princes to eat bitter wild berries in the mountains? You have grown old and senile, grandfather!'

Finding that none would heed his wise counsel, the old patriarch departed alone for the mountains.

A few weeks later, his prophecy was fulfilled to the letter.

The ram broke into the kitchen; a cook hurled a blazing brand from the hearth; the ram's thick wool ignited, and the shrieking, burning beast dashed into the royal stables! The dry straw exploded into a roaring inferno. Fifty royal warhorses were severely burned before the blaze was extinguished.

The King summoned his royal veterinary physicians in despair: 'Save my prize horses!'

The physicians consulted their medical scrolls and declared: 'Sire, the ancient treatises prescribe that the burns upon royal horses must be anointed with the warm fat of monkeys!'

The King ordered his guards to slaughter the troop of monkeys. In an instant, every pampered monkey in the palace was butchered to extract their fat.

Hearing of the massacre of his kin, the old patriarch wept, but resolved to avenge their deaths through intellect.

Wandering by a secluded mountain lake, the old monkey noticed strange tracks in the mud—human footprints leading down into the water, but none leading out! He deduced that an aquatic demon dwelt within the pool.

Using a hollow reed, the monkey drank safely from the water without stepping into the mud.

A hideous demon surfaced, wearing a necklace of human bones: 'I have devoured thousands who stepped into my waters, but your wit has preserved you! Ask any boon, and I will grant it!'

The monkey replied: 'Give me your pearl necklace. King Chandra and his courtiers are greedy for pearls. I will tell the King that this lake is paved with inexhaustible pearls, and lead him and his entire court to bathe in your waters!'

The demon gave him the pearl necklace.

The monkey returned to the palace wearing the dazzling pearls. Greedy for treasure, King Chandra, his ministers, and his army marched to the lake. The monkey instructed them: 'Enter all at once, dive deep, and gather the pearls!'

The entire court plunged into the water, and the hungry demon devoured them all!

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The wise man who foresees the fire departs the doomed abode,
And preserves his living breath along the mountain road;
While fools who mock the teacher's words to gorge on royal bread,
Supply the grease of medicine among the butchered dead."
moral: He who foresees an inevitable catastrophe and departs in time preserves his family, while the stubborn perish.

title: The Credulous Fiend
summary: In a quiet village lived an impoverished, bold weaver named Chandaka. While traveling through a dense, shadowy forest at nightfall, he wa...
full_text:
In a quiet village lived an impoverished, bold weaver named Chandaka. While traveling through a dense, shadowy forest at nightfall, he was confronted by a terrifying specter: an enormous, skeletal demon, or Rakshasa, with eyes like flaming braziers, sharp fangs projecting past his lips, and claws like curved iron sickles.

The demon roared with a voice like thunder: 'Prepare to die, mortal! I have not eaten meat in seven days, and I will devour your flesh on the spot!'

Any ordinary man would have fainted with terror, but the bold weaver summoned all his presence of mind. Instead of screaming or begging for mercy, he stood tall, planted his feet firmly upon the turf, folded his arms across his chest, and burst into a deafening roar of arrogant laughter: 'HAHAHAHA!'

The demon stopped in astonishment: 'Why do you laugh when you are about to be devoured?'

The weaver glared down upon him with contempt: 'Insolent mite! Do you think I am an ordinary mortal? I am a master demon-catcher! I carry an enchanted mirror in my pouch wherein I have already captured twenty-two ferocious demons like yourself! I came to this forest expressly to catch a twenty-third demon to complete my royal collection! Step closer, so that I may plunge you into the glass!'

Drawing a small polished brass mirror from his waistcloth, the weaver held it before the demon's face.

Peering into the polished metal in the twilight, the demon saw the terrifying reflection of a fierce, fanged face staring back at him with flaming eyes!

Believing that the glass already held a captive demon trapped inside, the gullible fiend fell to his knees in terror, trembling: 'Spare me, O mighty master! Do not imprison me in your glass! Command me as your humble slave, and I will serve you faithfully forever!'

The weaver put on a stern countenance: 'If you desire your freedom, swear by the sacred mountains that you will bring me a pot of gold dinars every morning, rebuild my house into a brick mansion, and never harm a soul in my village!'

The terrified demon swore the oath, carried the weaver home upon his shoulders, and delivered gold daily, making the bold weaver the richest man in the province.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"When supernatural peril strikes and terror fills the air,
A bold and unshakeable heart dissolves the darkest snare;
The weaver held his mirror up and made the demon bow,
Conquering the fiercest fiend with wit upon his brow."
moral: Presence of mind and bold bluster can terrify even a supernatural demon into servitude.

title: The Three-Breasted Princess
summary: In a northern kingdom ruled a great monarch whose queen gave birth to a daughter of exceptional beauty, but afflicted with an extraordina...
full_text:
In a northern kingdom ruled a great monarch whose queen gave birth to a daughter of exceptional beauty, but afflicted with an extraordinary physical anomaly: she was born with three breasts.

Horrified by the omen, the king consulted his royal astrologers, who declared: 'Sire, this princess brings misfortune to any king who marries her. Yet there is a prophecy: whichever husband she weds, the sight of him will cause the third breast to dissolve and vanish, restoring her to normal beauty!'

When the princess reached adulthood, the king, anxious to avoid foreign wars, issued a proclamation offering her hand with an enormous dowry to any man who would marry her without seeing her face beforehand.

In that city lived a sharp-witted, blind beggar named Andhaka, led by his hunchbacked companion, Kubja. Hearing of the vast dowry of gold and lands, the blind beggar agreed to wed the unknown maiden.

The marriage was celebrated with royal pomp. As the blind husband entered the bridal chamber, the princess looked upon him with compassionate acceptance, and in that instant, the prophecy was fulfilled: the superfluous third breast dissolved away, leaving her body as flawless and graceful as a celestial nymph!

The couple lived in wealth and comfort. But in time, the princess began to look down upon her blind husband and formed a secret affection for his hunchbacked companion, Kubja.

One afternoon, seeking to rid herself of the blind husband, the princess caught a venomous dead serpent in the garden, boiled its meat in a pot of savory milk porridge, and served it to the blind man, telling him it was a rare mountain delicacy.

As the blind man leaned over the steaming pot to eat, the hot, acrid fumes of the serpent's boiled venom rose into his face and eyes.

Suddenly, an agonizing burning seized his eyelids! The corrosive vapor dissolved the cataracts that had clouded his vision since childhood! Opening his eyes, the man cried out in astonishment: he could see!

Looking across the room, the restored husband saw his wife embracing the hunchback in the shadows.

Enraged by the betrayal, the husband seized the hunchback by his heels, swung him around like a sling, and hurled him against the stone wall! The hunchback struck the wall with his crooked back; the violent impact popped his twisted spine straight, so that he stood tall and erect!

Seeing her husband endowed with sight and her lover straightened into a handsome youth, the astonished princess confessed her error, and all three lived in harmony, marveling at the mysterious ways of destiny.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The tangled skein of destiny works through the darkest night,
Transforming venom into cure, and blindness into sight;
What seemed a curse of ancient days dissolves in sudden grace,
And leaves the hand of providence to govern time and place."
moral: What seems an abnormal misfortune ordained by fate can be resolved by destiny in its appointed time.

title: The Fiend Who Washed His Feet
summary: In a rural hamlet lived an honest, strong-willed Brahmin named Somadatta. While walking through a dense, shadowy forest at dusk, he was c...
keywords: the fiend who washed his feet
full_text:
In a rural hamlet lived an honest, strong-willed Brahmin named Somadatta. While walking through a dense, shadowy forest at dusk, he was confronted by a towering demon, or Rakshasa, who stepped from behind an ancient tree, declaring: 'I am a hungry forest demon! You must carry me across the river upon your broad shoulders!'

The demon leaped upon the Brahmin's shoulders, locking his long legs around the man's chest like an iron collar.

As Somadatta carried the heavy demon toward the riverbank, he noticed something extraordinary: the demon's feet resting against his chest were as smooth, clean, and tender as lotus petals, devoid of a single speck of dust!

The Brahmin asked: 'Brother demon, you wander through thorny jungles and muddy swamps; why are your feet as clean and tender as fresh butter?'

The demon replied with proud eccentricity: 'I am bound by a sacred vow of ritual purity: whenever my feet touch water or are washed, I am strictly forbidden to touch the earth or climb upon any creature until my feet are completely dry again!'

Somadatta noted this secret vulnerability in his mind.

Reaching the deep flowing river, the Brahmin waded waist-deep into the current. Pausing in mid-stream, he dipped both the demon's feet deep into the water, washing them thoroughly.

The Brahmin then gave a sudden, violent heave of his shoulders, hurling the demon off his back into the deep pool!

The demon tumbled into the water, shouting: 'Help! Carry me to the bank!'

The Brahmin scrambled quickly onto the dry riverbank and stood laughing: 'You told me your sacred vow forbids you to touch any living creature or climb upon my shoulders until your feet are completely dry! Stand in the water and wait for your feet to dry, demon!'

Trapped by his own sacred vow, unable to touch the Brahmin while his feet were wet, the demon was swept away by the swift river current, while the clever Brahmin walked home in safety and peace.

Thus Vishnu Sharma concluded the fifth scroll of wisdom:
"Observe the adversary's oath, his weakness, and his rule;
For by his own eccentric vow you can outwit the fool;
The Brahmin washed the demon's feet within the flowing stream,
And woke in triumph to behold the ending of the dream."
moral: Observe the eccentric vulnerabilities of an adversary; presence of mind turns his own weakness against him.
